newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters cooperate on picketing in Florida.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters cooperate on picketing in Florida.

text.p: UPS and a striking Teamsters union local agreed on Friday to new picketing rules for UPS facilities in south Florida, including an unusual collaboration that will allow Teamsters to picket UPS deliveries at shopping malls and elsewhere.

As part of a permanent injunction negotiated at the order of Dade County Circuit Judge Ronald Friedman, lawyers for UPS and Teamsters Local 769 agreed that striking UPS workers in seven Florida counties will not follow any UPS trucks making deliveries, but will instead each day have two pickets rendevous with one of the distinctively brown trucks at a prominent public site.
"UPS will advise the Teamsters of the public location, one in each county," said Howard Susskind, a lawyer for the Teamsters.

The injunction also allows as many as 10 strikers to picket 12 UPS centers and two large airports in Miami and West Palm Beach, but forbids violence against UPS staff and property, telephoning or otherwise contacting non-striking UPS workers and blocking the entrances to UPS facilities.
A non-striking UPS driver was stabbed last weekend north of Miami and six UPS strikers have been arrested.

Now in its 12th day, the strike against United Parcel Service of America Inc by 185,000 Teamsters union workers has crippled the operations of the world's largest package- delivery company and is disrupting many U.S. businesses. UPS has said the strike was costing it an estimated $300 million a week.

Central issues in national bargaining in Washington are a union demand that UPS convert part-time workers into full-time staff and a company demand the pensions of UPS workers be pulled out of a Teamster, multi-employer pension plan and put into a pension program just for UPS workers.

A Florida judge last week issued a preliminary injunction sharply limiting picketing by the Teamsters and forbidding the tracking of UPS trucks by strikers. Friedman, at a hearing on making the prohibitions permanent, ordered the rival lawyers to negotiate an agreement under a threat of imposing his own rules.
"Package vans were being followed by striking employees," William Hamilton, an attorney for UPS, told reporters after the hearing. "This had caused a dangerous situation for employees."

Friedman scolded both sides at the start of the hearing, saying the UPS lawyers wrongfully obtained the temporary restraining order a week ago without informing the Teamster attorneys and giving them a chance to make their case.
He criticized the Teamster lawyers for challenging the anti-violence portions of last week's order, even if only on questions of procedure.
"My number one concern is that there not be any acts of violence," the judge said.
